quote: Kann man allein mittelst der Cavallerischen Princips die Theorie der Flächenmessung in der Ebene u. im Raume für beliebig krumm be- grenzte Fläche und Körper begründen?
english: Can one ground the theory of area measurement in the plane and in space, for arbitrarily curvilinearly bounded surfaces and bodies, by means of Cavalieri's principle alone?
topic: The page covers four short notes: when cos(2π/n) is rational, extending the Gauss-integral-theorem treatment of divergence to oblique curvilinear coordinates, expressing a continuous function through its iterated integrals, and whether Cavalieri's principle alone can ground the theory of area and volume.

triage.modern_statement: Take a volume functional (or area functional) on a class of plane regions and solids that may have arbitrary curved boundaries. Suppose it is invariant under congruence, additive, and normalised on the unit square or cube. Is it then completely determined if, besides elementary decomposition, the only extra axiom is Cavalieri's principle? That principle says that two figures whose sections by every parallel line or plane at the same height have equal length or area also have equal area or volume. Put another way: can Cavalieri's principle, with no exhaustion or limit arguments, replace the limit processes otherwise needed to measure curvilinear figures? This is a question about the foundations of elementary measure theory.
triage.answered_by: I found no source that answers this exact question (Cavalieri's principle as the only non-elementary axiom, applied to arbitrary curved figures). The closest well-known result is Hilbert's third problem (ICM 1900), solved by Max Dehn in 1901/1902. He showed that scissors-congruence alone cannot ground the volume of polyhedra, so some continuity-type principle such as exhaustion or Cavalieri is unavoidable. In modern measure theory (Jordan–Peano content, Lebesgue measure, Fubini 1907), Cavalieri's principle is a theorem derived from the measure, not an axiom that grounds it.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's third problem is the published problem about whether volume theory, even for polyhedra, can be grounded without limiting processes. Every proof of the tetrahedron volume formula uses some limit argument, such as exhaustion or calculus.

Dehn answered the third problem: a regular tetrahedron and a cube of the same volume are not scissors congruent. So for polyhedra, decomposition alone is not enough and a continuity principle is needed.
Hilbert's ICM 1900 wording of the third problem refers to two tetrahedra with equal bases and equal altitudes. These are exactly the figures Cavalieri's principle makes equal in volume.
In modern treatments, Cavalieri's principle is proved as a theorem about Lebesgue measure (area or volume defined as Lebesgue measure), not used as a founding axiom.
Fubini proved the general result in 1907. Cavalieri's principle is described as an earlier special case.

triage.why: The note is a real foundational question, but it is phrased loosely and I found no paper that poses or answers it in this form. It is clearly related to Hilbert's third problem: the third problem asks whether a continuity principle can be avoided for polyhedra, and Dehn showed it cannot. This note asks the other way round, whether Cavalieri's principle by itself is enough even for curved figures. Hilbert's third problem is still studied (Dehn invariants, scissors-congruence groups), but that is not this question. I am not labelling it as the third problem, and I am not calling it solved without a source. Modern measure theory gets around the question by defining measure through limits and then deriving Cavalieri as a theorem.
